prompt: Which section of the `hits` binary does the Go runtime read while the program runs, to print a stack trace or to grow a goroutine's stack?
hint: One of them maps every instruction address to a function, a file and a line.

choices.text: `.debug_info`, the DWARF description of every function
choices.why: DWARF sits at address 0: it is never loaded into memory, so the running program cannot read it. Debuggers read it from the file.

choices.text: `.gopclntab`
choices.why: Right. It maps addresses to functions, files and lines and records frame sizes; the runtime walks stacks with it, which is why no flag removes it.

choices.text: `.symtab`, the ELF symbol table
choices.why: The symbol table is for tools outside the program, like `nm` and `gdb`. It is not loaded either, and a stripped binary still prints stack traces without it.

choices.text: `.bss`
choices.why: `.bss` is zeroed memory for variables, with no bytes in the file. It holds no names and no line numbers.

prompt: The default build of `hits` is 4,031,935 bytes, and its eight `.debug_` sections add up to 1,162,307. To the nearest whole number, what percentage of the file is DWARF?
hint: Divide, multiply by 100, round.

prompt: Match each part of the `hits` binary with who reads it.
hint: Ask whether the part is loaded into memory at all.

pairs.right: the Go runtime, walking a stack
a debugger such as `gdb` or Delve

prompt: `go tool nm` counts 3,886 symbols in `hits`, and only ten functions are from `hits` itself. A colleague concludes that every Go binary carries the whole standard library. What do the measurements say?
hint: Look at which packages showed up in the sums, and what `tally.Parse` calls.

choices.text: He is right: the standard library is linked whole, so the size is fixed whatever the program does
choices.why: Section 05's three programs differ by more than a megabyte, from 1,310,880 to 2,568,352 bytes, and they differ only in what they import.

choices.text: Only the runtime is shared; standard packages are compiled into a separate shared library
choices.why: The binary is statically linked and `file` says so. `time.parse` and `encoding/json` appear as code inside it.

choices.text: What is in it is what `hits` reaches: `time` through `tally.Parse`, `encoding/json` through `-json`
choices.why: Right. The runtime is always there, and the rest follows the imports: `time.parse` is the largest function because `Parse` calls it, and JSON is there for two flags.

choices.text: The 3,886 symbols are mostly DWARF entries, not code
choices.why: `go tool nm` reads the ELF symbol table, not DWARF, and the letters `T` and `t` mark code. The runtime alone is 438,417 bytes of it.

prompt: What does `-ldflags="-w"` remove from the `hits` binary?
hint: It saved 1,162,426 bytes.

choices.text: The DWARF that a debugger like gdb reads
choices.why: Right. 1,162,426 bytes is within 119 of what the eight `.debug_` sections added up to.

choices.text: The table the runtime uses to name functions in a stack trace
choices.why: That is `.gopclntab`, and it was still there: the stripped binary named every function when it got `SIGQUIT`.

choices.text: The file paths of the build machine
choices.why: That is `-trimpath`, a flag of `go build` itself, and it saved 5,042 bytes rather than a megabyte.

choices.text: Every function that `main` never calls
choices.why: The linker leaves out unreachable functions in every build, flags or not. `-w` touches no code.

prompt: A build script passes only `-ldflags=-s`. Does the binary still carry DWARF?
hint: Compare the sizes of the `-s` and `-s -w` builds, and what `go doc cmd/link` says.

choices.text: Yes, because `-s` removes only the symbol table, as the short help says
choices.why: The short help is incomplete. The `-s` build came out at exactly the size of `-s -w`, 2,654,368 bytes.

choices.text: No: `-s` implies `-w` unless the script adds `-w=0`
choices.why: Right. `go doc cmd/link` says so, and `-s -w=0` put 1,162,362 bytes of DWARF back.

choices.text: Only on Linux; on macOS and Windows `-w` has to be given as well
choices.why: Nothing in the documentation makes the rule depend on the system, and this lesson measured Linux only. The rule is the linker's.

choices.text: It depends on `-trimpath`, which decides whether debugging information is kept
choices.why: `-trimpath` rewrites paths and saved 5,042 bytes. Whether DWARF is written is up to `-s` and `-w`.

prompt: `hits`, built with `-trimpath -ldflags="-s -w"`, gets `SIGQUIT` while it reads standard input. What does the frame for `main.main` look like?
hint: Which table names functions for the runtime, and what did `-trimpath` do to the paths?

choices.text: `main.main()` with `example.com/hits/main.go:28` under it
choices.why: Right. `.gopclntab` survives stripping, and `-trimpath` turned `/home/ana/small/main.go` into a path that starts with the module.

choices.text: Bare addresses such as `pc=0x52b60c`, because the names went with the symbol table
choices.why: The names a stack trace prints come from `.gopclntab`, which no flag removes. The symbol table is for tools like `nm`.

choices.text: `main.main()` with `/home/ana/small/main.go:28` under it
choices.why: That is the default build's frame. `-trimpath` replaces the directory with the module path.

choices.text: No trace at all: a stripped binary just exits on `SIGQUIT`
choices.why: The stripped build printed every goroutine's stack, from `tally.Count` down to `main.main`.

prompt: `strings hits | grep -c /home/ana` printed 2 for the default build and 0 for the build made with `go build ___`.
hint: A flag of `go build` itself, not of the linker, that rewrites recorded file names.

prompt: Version v1.4.0 of a tool ships built with `-s -w`. A customer's copy crashes, and you want to step through the failing function in `gdb`. What should the release process have done for this to be possible?
hint: gdb needs the parts `-s -w` removed, from a build of exactly the same code.

choices.text: Nothing: `gdb` can read the stack trace's function names from `.gopclntab`
choices.why: `gdb` printed `No symbol table is loaded` on the stripped build. It reads DWARF and the symbol table, not the runtime's table.

choices.text: Kept the unstripped binary built from the same commit
choices.why: Right. The stripped and unstripped builds hold the same code; the second carries the DWARF and symbols `gdb` needs.

choices.text: Built with `-trimpath`, so that `gdb` finds the source files by module path
choices.why: `-trimpath` changes paths and leaves the DWARF question alone; with `-s -w` there is still no debugging information.

choices.text: Recorded `go version -m` output, from which the symbols can be rebuilt
choices.why: `go version -m` lists the module, the settings and the revision. It holds no symbols and no line tables.

prompt: `go build -ldflags="-X main.Version=v1.1.0"` succeeds, and `./hits version` still prints `hits dev`. Why?
hint: Look at how the variable is spelt in `version.go`.

choices.text: The variable is `version`, and `-X` ignores a name it cannot find
choices.why: Right. Go names are case-sensitive, and the linker gave no warning; a release script has to check the output itself.

choices.text: `-X` only works when the tree has been committed and tagged
choices.why: The earlier build with `-X main.version=v1.1.0` set the name on a dirty tree. `-X` does not read git at all.

choices.text: `-X` sets constants, and `version` is a variable
choices.why: It is the other way round: `-X` sets string variables and cannot touch a `const`.

choices.text: The value has to be quoted twice inside `-ldflags`
choices.why: The same quoting with the lower-case name worked. The difference between the two builds is one letter.

prompt: Which of these declarations in package `main` can `-ldflags="-X main.name=v2"` set? Choose all that apply.
hint: `go doc cmd/link` states the condition in two sentences.

choices.text: `var name string`
choices.why: Right. An uninitialised string variable is one of the two cases the documentation names.

choices.text: `var name = "dev"`
choices.why: Right. A string variable initialised to a constant expression is the other case, and it is how `version.go` declares `version`.

choices.text: `const name = "dev"`
choices.why: A constant has no storage for the linker to fill in. `-X` sets variables only.

choices.text: `var name = strings.ToLower("DEV")`
choices.why: The documentation says `-X` does not work when the initializer makes a function call.

choices.text: `var name int`
choices.why: `-X` sets string variables; the value on the command line is text.

prompt: Put in order the steps that produce a `hits` binary that reports itself as `v1.2.0`, with no DWARF and no home directory in it.
hint: The tag names a commit, and the build reads the tag.

prompt: A build server downloads a source archive of tag v1.1.0, with no `.git` directory, and runs a plain `go build`. What does `./hits version` print on its second line?
hint: Where does the go command get the module version from?

choices.text: `module example.com/hits v1.1.0, go1.27.1`, read from the archive's name
choices.why: The go command takes the version from version control, not from a directory or archive name.

choices.text: `module example.com/hits (devel), go1.27.1`, and no `vcs` lines after it
choices.why: Right. That is what the build in `/tmp/small-v1.1.0` printed; only `-X` could still have named the release.

choices.text: Nothing: the build fails, because `-buildvcs` requires a repository
choices.why: In its default mode, `auto`, the go command stamps what it finds and builds anyway; only `-buildvcs=true` turns the absence into an error.

choices.text: `module example.com/hits v1.1.0+dirty`, because the files are not in a commit
choices.why: `+dirty` marks a repository with uncommitted changes. With no repository there is nothing to compare against, and no version either.

prompt: UPX took `hits` from 2,666,656 to 1,140,620 bytes. What does the smaller file cost?
hint: Look at the hundred starts, and at `go version -m`.

choices.text: Every start pays for decompressing, and `go version -m` cannot read it
choices.why: Right. A hundred starts took 2.182 seconds against 0.270, and `go version -m` said `not a Go executable`.

choices.text: Nothing at run time; only the build takes longer
choices.why: The decompressor runs inside every start of the program. That is where the 2.182 seconds came from.

choices.text: It counts the log more slowly, because the code stays compressed in memory
choices.why: The program is rebuilt in memory before it runs and then runs as before; the measured cost is the start.

choices.text: It no longer runs on other Linux machines
choices.why: A UPX file is still an ordinary executable for the same system and processor; it carries its own decompressor.

prompt: Built with `-s -w`, a program that only writes `hello` to standard output is 1,310,880 bytes, and the same program encoding the word with `encoding/json` is 2,568,352. How many bytes does the import add?
hint: Subtract.

prompt: What is the difference between `go build -gcflags=-l` and `go build -gcflags=all=-l`?
hint: One of them reaches the standard library.

choices.text: None; `all=` is an older spelling
choices.why: The prefix is a package pattern. Without one, the flag goes only to the packages named on the command line.

choices.text: The first applies to the packages named on the command line, the second to every package
choices.why: Right. Without `all=`, only `main` would lose inlining here, and the runtime and the standard library would not.

choices.text: The first goes to the linker, the second to the compiler
choices.why: Both go to the compiler; `-ldflags` is the one for the linker.

choices.text: `all=` also strips the symbol table
choices.why: Stripping is the linker's `-s`. `all=` only widens which packages get `-l`.

prompt: A tool is downloaded as a `.tar.gz`, and its maintainer proposes adding UPX to the release to make the download smaller. Going by the `hits` measurements, what will it buy?
hint: Compare `gzip -9` on the plain binary and on the UPX one.

choices.text: Half the download, since UPX shrank the binary to 43%
choices.why: That was against the uncompressed file. `gzip -9` already brought the plain binary to 1,171,128 bytes.

choices.text: Nothing either way, because `gzip` undoes UPX
choices.why: `gzip` does not undo anything; it compresses the UPX file a little further, to 1,118,110 bytes.

choices.text: A few per cent off the archive, for a slower start on every run
choices.why: Right. 1,118,110 bytes against 1,171,128 is under 5%, and every start pays the decompression.

choices.text: A smaller download and a faster start, since less is read from disk
choices.why: The start measured about eight times slower: decompressing costs far more than reading a few hundred kilobytes.

prompt: In this lab, `podman run --rm docker.io/library/busybox:1.36 echo ok` fails with a message about `/dev/net/tun`, and the same command with `--network=none` prints `ok`. Why?
hint: Which program builds a rootless container's network, and what did `stat` say about the device?

choices.text: Podman is not installed correctly and must be reinstalled
choices.why: The container started and printed `ok` with `--network=none`; Podman works.

choices.text: busybox needs a network to start up, and this sandbox machine has no network at all
choices.why: busybox started without any network. What failed was setting one up.

choices.text: `slirp4netns` opens `/dev/net/tun`, which only root is allowed to open here
choices.why: Right. `stat` showed `crw------- root`; with no network asked for, `slirp4netns` is never started.

choices.text: Ana has no range in `/etc/subuid`
choices.why: `grep` found her range, 165536 and 65,536 ids, and a missing range fails with a different message.

prompt: A brand-new account's first container fails: the log says no id ranges were found for the user, then `insufficient UIDs or GIDs`. What fixes it?
hint: Two steps: one as root, one as the account.

choices.text: Running `podman` with `sudo`
choices.why: That would run the container as root, the thing rootless Podman exists to avoid; the account's own setup stays broken.

choices.text: A range for the user in `/etc/subuid` and `/etc/subgid`, then `podman system migrate`
choices.why: Right. `usermod --add-subuids` and `--add-subgids` write the range, and `migrate` makes Podman pick it up.

choices.text: Adding `--network=none` to the command, which skips the user namespace and its id mapping
choices.why: `--network=none` avoids the `/dev/net/tun` problem and nothing else. The user namespace is set up either way, and this failure is about its ids.

choices.text: Pulling a smaller image with fewer files
choices.why: The size is irrelevant: busybox failed because one of its owners, id 65534, had nothing to map to.

prompt: `/etc/subuid` has the line `ana:165536:65536`. What is the first id after the end of Ana's range, where a new account's range can start without overlapping hers?
hint: Start plus length.

prompt: A colleague installs Docker Engine and adds every developer to the `docker` group so that nobody has to type `sudo`. What has he given them?
hint: Who does the work when a member of the group runs `docker run`?

choices.text: The same as rootless Podman: containers that belong to each user
choices.why: Podman's containers are started by the user's own process. Docker's are started by a daemon running as root, on behalf of whoever may ask it.

choices.text: Access to the daemon's socket only, which cannot affect the host
choices.why: The daemon runs as root and does what it is asked, including mounting the host's files into a container; being allowed to ask is the power.

choices.text: Nothing beyond what `sudo` already gave them, since they had to type a password for it
choices.why: Group membership needs no password at each use, and it reaches a root daemon directly.

choices.text: The equivalent of root on that machine
choices.why: Right. Asking a root daemon to run anything is root by another route, which is the reason this course uses rootless Podman.

prompt: Match each flag with what it did to `hits`.
hint: Four belong to the build of section 03 or 04; one to section 05.

pairs.right: removed the symbol table, and the DWARF with it
set a string variable at link time
turned inlining off in every package

prompt: On a server you find a Linux executable that runs and answers like a Go tool, but `go version -m` says `not a Go executable` and `go tool nm` finds no symbols. What is the likeliest explanation?
hint: One thing measured in this lesson hides the build information, and one removes the symbols.

choices.text: It was built with `-s -w`, which removes the build information
choices.why: A `-s -w` build still answered `go version -m`: the build information has a section of its own that `-s` leaves alone.

choices.text: It was compiled with `-trimpath`
choices.why: `-trimpath` rewrites paths; the trimmed builds kept both their symbols and their build information.

choices.text: It was packed with UPX after the build
choices.why: Right. UPX compresses everything, build information and symbols included, and `go version -m` on the UPX file of `hits` said exactly `not a Go executable`.

choices.text: It was built from a source archive with no `.git`
choices.why: Such a build still has build information, with `(devel)` as its version, and `go version -m` reads it.

prompt: To set the string variable `version` of the program's `main` package to v2.0.0 while linking, the build passes `-ldflags="-X ___=v2.0.0"`.
hint: The package path, a dot, and the variable's name, with the case exactly as declared.
